passages.title: The Rediscovery of Wild Apples
passages.blurb: Read the text and answer questions 1–13.

paragraphs.text: High in the Tien Shan mountains of Central Asia grow forests of wild apple trees that botanists now believe to be the ancestor of every cultivated apple on Earth. For decades these forests were largely unknown to Western science, hidden behind closed borders and dismissed as ornamental curiosities rather than a genetic treasure house.

The pioneering work of the Russian botanist Nikolai Vavilov in the 1920s first drew attention to the region. Travelling through the valleys around Almaty, he was astonished to find trees bearing fruit almost indistinguishable from the apples sold in European markets. Vavilov proposed that the diversity of a crop is greatest at its place of origin, and the apple, he concluded, had begun here.

Modern DNA analysis has confirmed his intuition. Studies comparing the wild Malus sieversii with domestic varieties show that the cultivated apple is, genetically, almost the same species. Over thousands of years, fruit was carried west along trade routes, and chance crossings with European crab apples added only a small fraction to the genome.

The significance of the wild forests is not merely historical. Cultivated apples have become genetically narrow, bred for sweetness, colour and shelf life at the expense of resistance to disease. The wild trees, by contrast, harbour an enormous range of traits — some resist fungal infection, others tolerate drought or extreme cold.

Yet the forests are under threat. Grazing livestock strip away seedlings before they can mature, and orchards and housing have replaced large areas of woodland. Conservationists warn that without protection, a resource that took millions of years to evolve could vanish within a generation.

Efforts are now under way to catalogue and preserve the wild apples. Seed banks have collected samples, and protected reserves have been established. Breeders hope that genes drawn from these ancient trees will one day produce orchard varieties that need far fewer chemical sprays.

passages.title: Designing Cities for the Heat
passages.subtitle: How urban planners are adapting to rising temperatures
passages.blurb: Read the text and answer questions 14–26.

paragraphs.text: As average temperatures climb, planners are rethinking the very fabric of cities. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, producing the well-documented 'urban heat island' effect that can leave city centres several degrees warmer than their rural surroundings.

One of the simplest interventions is also among the oldest: trees. A mature street tree can transpire hundreds of litres of water on a hot day, cooling the air much as sweating cools the body. Studies in several cities have found that well-shaded streets can be up to five degrees cooler than bare ones.

Surfaces matter too. Dark roofs can reach temperatures hot enough to fry an egg, while pale or reflective coatings stay markedly cooler. Painting roofs white is cheap, and on a large scale it can lower a neighbourhood's temperature measurably, reducing the demand for air conditioning.

Water features, from fountains to restored streams, provide localised cooling through evaporation. Historically, many hot-climate cities were built around courtyards and channels precisely for this reason, a wisdom that modern engineering had, until recently, largely forgotten.

Not every solution is purely technical. The way streets are oriented can funnel cooling breezes or block them entirely. Narrow lanes that shade one another work well in some climates but trap pollutants in others, so context is everything.

Critics caution that piecemeal measures are not enough. Without coordinated policy, the benefits of a shady park in one district do little for residents elsewhere, and the poorest neighbourhoods — often the hottest — are the least likely to receive investment.

passages.title: The Science of Persuasion
passages.blurb: Read the text and answer questions 27–40.

paragraphs.text: For more than half a century, psychologists have tried to pin down what makes one message persuasive and another forgettable. The earliest models assumed that people weigh arguments rationally, accepting whichever case is logically stronger. Decades of experiments have shown that the reality is far messier.

A landmark idea is the so-called dual-process account, which holds that we think in two distinct ways. One is fast, intuitive and effortless; the other is slow, deliberate and demanding. Persuasion, on this view, can travel by either route. A careful reader may scrutinise every claim, while a distracted one is swayed by surface cues — the confidence of a speaker, the gloss of a brochure.

Crucially, which route dominates depends on motivation and capacity. When a decision matters and we have time to think, we engage the slow system and argument quality wins out. When we are busy, tired or indifferent, shortcuts take over. Advertisers have long exploited this, pairing products with attractive faces rather than evidence.

Source credibility complicates the picture further. An expert's words carry weight, but only up to a point; audiences quickly discount a source they suspect of self-interest. Interestingly, a message can become more persuasive when the listener forgets where it came from — a phenomenon researchers call the 'sleeper effect'.

Emotion, too, is no mere distraction. Moderate fear can spur action, but only when paired with a clear, achievable recommendation; without one, frightened audiences tend to switch off entirely. The most durable attitude change, studies suggest, comes not from being told what to think but from being led to generate the arguments oneself.
